questions.stem: According to VSEPR theory, what determines the shape of a molecule?
options: The number of neutrons in the nucleus of the central atom of the molecule
The order in which the atoms were joined when the molecule was formed
Repulsion between electron pairs in the valence shell of the central atom
Attraction between the nuclei of neighbouring molecules in the substance
questions.explanation: Valence shell electron pair repulsion theory says that bonding pairs and lone pairs around the central atom repel each other and spread out as far apart as possible. Attractions between molecules are intermolecular forces and do not set the shape of a single molecule.

questions.stem: Methane, CH₄, has four bonding pairs and no lone pairs around carbon. What are its shape and H-C-H bond angle?
options: Pyramidal, 107°
Tetrahedral, 109.5°
Trigonal planar, 120°
Square planar, 90°
questions.explanation: Four electron pairs around a central atom spread out to the corners of a tetrahedron, giving bond angles of 109.5°. A flat square arrangement at 90° would put the pairs closer together than a tetrahedron does.

questions.stem: Ammonia, NH₃, has three bonding pairs and one lone pair on nitrogen. What is the shape of the molecule?
options: Bent
Pyramidal
Trigonal planar
Tetrahedral
questions.explanation: The four electron pairs are arranged tetrahedrally, but shape is named from the positions of the atoms only, so three hydrogen atoms around nitrogen give a pyramid. Trigonal planar would need three electron pairs and no lone pair on the central atom.

questions.stem: Why is the H-O-H bond angle in water (about 104.5°) smaller than the H-C-H angle in methane (109.5°)?
options: Hydrogen bonds between water molecules pull the hydrogen atoms closer together
The O-H bonds in water are much longer than the C-H bonds in methane
Two lone pairs on oxygen repel the bonding pairs more strongly than bonding pairs do
Oxygen has fewer electron pairs around it than carbon has in methane
questions.explanation: Both central atoms have four electron pairs, but oxygen has two lone pairs. Lone pairs are held closer to the nucleus and repel more strongly than bonding pairs, squeezing the bond angle. Hydrogen bonds are between molecules and do not set the angle within a molecule.

questions.stem: Boron trifluoride, BF₃, has three bonding pairs and no lone pairs on boron. What are its shape and F-B-F bond angle?
options: Tetrahedral, 109.5°
Trigonal planar, 120°
Pyramidal, 107°
questions.explanation: Three electron pairs spread out in a flat triangle around boron, 120° apart. A pyramidal shape needs a lone pair on the central atom as well as three bonding pairs, and boron in BF₃ has none.

questions.stem: Carbon dioxide, O=C=O, has two double bonds and no lone pairs on carbon. What is its shape?
options: Bent, with a bond angle of 104.5°
Trigonal planar, with angles of 120°
Tetrahedral, with angles of 109.5°
Linear, with a bond angle of 180°
questions.explanation: In VSEPR theory a double bond counts as one region of electron density, so carbon has two regions that point in opposite directions, giving a linear molecule. A bent shape arises when the central atom also has lone pairs, as in water.

questions.stem: Hydrogen sulfide, H₂S, has a central sulfur atom with two bonding pairs and two lone pairs. Which statement about H₂S is correct?
options: It is bent and polar, like water
It is linear and non-polar, like carbon dioxide
It is bent but non-polar, as S and H share electrons equally
It is pyramidal and polar, like ammonia
questions.explanation: Sulfur is in the same group as oxygen and, like water, has two bonding pairs and two lone pairs, so H₂S is bent. The S-H bonds are slightly polar and the bent shape means the dipoles do not cancel, so the molecule is polar.

questions.stem: What makes a covalent bond polar?
options: The bond contains more than one shared pair
The bond is between two metal atoms
The two bonded atoms differ in electronegativity
The two bonded atoms are of the same element
questions.explanation: When one atom attracts the shared electrons more strongly than the other, the electrons spend more time near it, giving partial charges. Atoms of the same element have equal electronegativity and form non-polar bonds, whatever the number of shared pairs.

questions.stem: Carbon tetrachloride, CCl₄, contains four polar C-Cl bonds but is a non-polar molecule. Why?
options: Its lone pairs on carbon balance the polar bonds
Its molecules are too large to have a dipole
Its tetrahedral shape is symmetrical, so the bond dipoles cancel
Carbon and chlorine have identical electronegativities
questions.explanation: Each C-Cl bond is polar, but the four bonds point to the corners of a regular tetrahedron and their dipoles cancel. Chlorine is more electronegative than carbon, so the bonds themselves are polar, and carbon in CCl₄ has no lone pairs.

questions.stem: Which molecule is polar?
options: Carbon dioxide, CO₂
Trichloromethane, CHCl₃
Methane, CH₄
Boron trifluoride, BF₃
questions.explanation: In CHCl₃ one corner of the tetrahedron holds hydrogen instead of chlorine, so the bond dipoles do not cancel and the molecule is polar. CH₄, BF₃ and CO₂ are symmetrical, so any bond dipoles cancel.

questions.stem: Phosphorus trichloride, PCl₃, and boron trichloride, BCl₃, both contain three polar bonds to chlorine. Which statement explains the difference in their polarity?
options: PCl₃ is trigonal planar, so it is polar; BCl₃ is pyramidal with a lone pair, so it is non-polar
Both are pyramidal, but P-Cl bonds are polar while B-Cl bonds are non-polar
Both are trigonal planar, but phosphorus is more electronegative than chlorine
PCl₃ is pyramidal with a lone pair, so it is polar; BCl₃ is trigonal planar, so it is non-polar
questions.explanation: Phosphorus has a lone pair as well as three bonding pairs, so PCl₃ is pyramidal and its bond dipoles do not cancel. Boron has only three bonding pairs, so BCl₃ is flat and symmetrical and its dipoles cancel. Chlorine is more electronegative than both phosphorus and boron.

questions.stem: Which intermolecular force acts between all molecules, polar and non-polar?
options: Dispersion forces
Hydrogen bonding
Dipole-dipole attractions
Ionic bonding
questions.explanation: Dispersion forces arise from temporary dipoles caused by the movement of electrons, so every molecule has them. Dipole-dipole attractions need a permanent dipole, and hydrogen bonding needs H bonded to N, O or F.

questions.stem: Hydrogen bonding between molecules occurs when a hydrogen atom is covalently bonded to:
options: nitrogen, oxygen or fluorine
carbon, sulfur or chlorine
any non-metal atom
a metal atom
questions.explanation: Nitrogen, oxygen and fluorine are small and highly electronegative, so an H atom bonded to them carries a large partial positive charge that is attracted to a lone pair on N, O or F in a neighbouring molecule. A C-H bond is barely polar and does not form hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: The boiling points of the halogens increase from F₂ (−188 °C) to Cl₂ (−34 °C) to Br₂ (59 °C). What explains this trend?
options: The covalent bond within each molecule becomes stronger down the group
The molecules become more polar down the group, increasing dipole-dipole forces
Hydrogen bonding becomes stronger as the halogen atom becomes larger
Larger molecules with more electrons have stronger dispersion forces
questions.explanation: Halogen molecules are non-polar, so only dispersion forces act between them, and these grow with the number of electrons. Boiling separates molecules from each other; it does not break the bond inside each molecule.

questions.stem: Water (M = 18) boils at 100 °C, but methane (M = 16) boils at −162 °C. What is the main reason for the difference?
options: Hydrogen bonding between water molecules is much stronger than dispersion forces between methane molecules
O-H covalent bonds must be broken to boil water, but C-H bonds are not broken when methane boils
Water molecules have a much larger molar mass, so their dispersion forces are much stronger
Methane molecules are polar and repel each other, so they separate at a much lower temperature
questions.explanation: The two molecules have similar masses and numbers of electrons, so the difference comes from hydrogen bonding between water molecules. No covalent bonds are broken when either substance boils.

questions.stem: Ethanol, CH₃CH₂OH, and methoxymethane, CH₃OCH₃, have the same molecular formula. Ethanol boils at 78 °C and methoxymethane at −24 °C. Why?
options: Ethanol has more electrons, so its dispersion forces are much stronger
Methoxymethane has an O-H group, which weakens the forces between molecules
Ethanol has an O-H group, so its molecules form hydrogen bonds with each other
Methoxymethane is non-polar, so only dispersion forces act between its molecules
questions.explanation: Only ethanol has hydrogen bonded directly to oxygen, so ethanol molecules hydrogen bond to each other. Methoxymethane is bent at oxygen and is polar, so it has dipole-dipole forces, but these are weaker. The two isomers have identical numbers of electrons.

questions.stem: HCl, HBr and HI have boiling points of −85 °C, −67 °C and −35 °C. The H-X bond becomes less polar from HCl to HI. What do these data show?
options: Hydrogen bonding, which is strongest in HI, has the greater effect here
The H-X covalent bond strength, which rises down the group, has the greater effect here
Dispersion forces, which increase with molecular size, have the greater effect here
Dipole-dipole forces, which increase as polarity falls, have the greater effect here
questions.explanation: If dipole-dipole forces dominated, boiling points would fall as the bonds became less polar. Instead they rise, because dispersion forces grow with the number of electrons and outweigh the drop in polarity. None of these molecules form hydrogen bonds.

questions.stem: At 20 °C, propanone has a much higher vapour pressure than water. What does this indicate?
options: Propanone has a higher boiling point than water
The intermolecular forces in propanone are weaker than those in water
The intermolecular forces in propanone are stronger than those in water
Propanone molecules are heavier than water molecules
questions.explanation: A higher vapour pressure means more molecules escape from the liquid surface at a given temperature, which happens when the forces holding molecules together are weaker. A liquid with weaker forces and higher vapour pressure has a lower boiling point.

questions.stem: As the strength of the intermolecular forces in a molecular substance increases, its boiling point:
options: falls and its vapour pressure rises
rises and its vapour pressure falls
rises and its vapour pressure rises
falls and its vapour pressure falls
questions.explanation: Stronger forces between molecules need more energy to overcome, so the boiling point rises. Fewer molecules escape from the surface at any given temperature, so the vapour pressure is lower.

questions.stem: Ethanol mixes with water in all proportions, but hexane does not dissolve in water. Why?
options: Ethanol can hydrogen bond with water molecules, but hexane can form only dispersion forces
Ethanol is an ionic compound that dissociates in water, but hexane is molecular
Hexane molecules are polar and repel the polar water molecules
Hexane reacts with water to form an insoluble layer on the surface
questions.explanation: Ethanol's O-H group forms hydrogen bonds with water, replacing the water-water hydrogen bonds that are broken when it dissolves. Hexane is non-polar, and its weak attractions to water cannot compensate for breaking hydrogen bonds between water molecules. Ethanol is molecular, not ionic.

questions.stem: Which list places these substances in order of increasing boiling point: butane C₄H₁₀, propan-1-ol C₃H₇OH, methane CH₄?
options: Methane, propan-1-ol, butane
Propan-1-ol, butane, methane
Methane, butane, propan-1-ol
Butane, methane, propan-1-ol
questions.explanation: Methane and butane are non-polar, and butane has more electrons, so it has stronger dispersion forces and a higher boiling point than methane. Propan-1-ol has a similar number of electrons to butane but also forms hydrogen bonds, so it boils highest.

questions.stem: In paper or thin layer chromatography, what does a component that is strongly attracted to the stationary phase do?
options: Moves close to the solvent front, giving a high Rf value
Moves with the solvent, giving an Rf value of exactly 1
Moves below the baseline, giving a negative Rf value
Moves only a short distance, giving a low Rf value
questions.explanation: Separation depends on the balance between attraction to the stationary phase and solubility in the mobile phase. A component held strongly by the stationary phase spends less time moving with the solvent, so it travels a short distance.

questions.stem: In a thin layer chromatogram, a spot travels 3.6 cm from the baseline while the solvent front travels 9.0 cm. What is the Rf value of the spot?
questions.explanation: Rf = distance moved by the spot ÷ distance moved by the solvent front = 3.6 ÷ 9.0 = 0.40. Dividing the other way gives 2.5, but Rf can never be greater than 1 because a spot cannot travel further than the solvent.

questions.stem: A dye has an Rf value of 0.25 in a particular solvent. If the solvent front travels 12.0 cm, how far will the dye travel from the baseline?
options: 4.8 cm
9.0 cm
48 cm
3.0 cm
questions.explanation: Rearranging Rf = spot distance ÷ solvent distance gives spot distance = 0.25 × 12.0 = 3.0 cm. A distance of 9.0 cm is how far the dye falls short of the solvent front.

questions.stem: A sample of a food colouring produces three spots on a paper chromatogram. What can be concluded?
options: The colouring is a pure substance with three isomers
The colouring contains exactly three elements
The colouring reacted with the paper in three places
The colouring is a mixture of at least three substances
questions.explanation: Each separate spot is a different component, so the colouring is a mixture of at least three substances. It could contain more, because two components with the same Rf in this solvent would appear as one spot. Chromatography separates compounds, not elements.

questions.stem: An unknown sample gives one spot with Rf 0.52. A standard of caffeine run on the same plate in the same solvent also gives Rf 0.52. What is the best conclusion?
options: The sample may be caffeine; running both in a second solvent would strengthen this
The sample is certainly pure caffeine, because one spot always means a pure substance
The sample cannot be caffeine, because a sample and a standard never give the same Rf
The sample is a mixture, because the Rf value is close to one half
questions.explanation: Matching Rf values under identical conditions suggest the sample is caffeine, but a different substance could have the same Rf in that solvent. Matching again in a second solvent with different polarity makes the identification more reliable.

questions.stem: Silica, the stationary phase on a TLC plate, is very polar. Using a non-polar solvent, which component of a mixture will travel furthest?
options: The component that is most soluble in water
The least polar component
The most polar component
The component with the most O-H groups
questions.explanation: A non-polar component is attracted only weakly to polar silica and dissolves well in the non-polar mobile phase, so it moves furthest. Polar components, especially those with O-H groups, adsorb strongly to the silica and lag behind.

questions.stem: Why is the baseline on a paper chromatogram drawn in pencil and placed above the level of the solvent?
options: Pencil absorbs the solvent faster, and spots placed higher travel more slowly
Pencil does not dissolve in the solvent, and the spots must not dissolve into the solvent pool
Pencil makes the paper more polar, and the solvent must not wet the baseline
Ink would react with the solvent, and the spots must start below the solvent level
questions.explanation: Graphite is insoluble, so a pencil line does not run and add extra spots. If the baseline were below the solvent surface, the sample spots would dissolve into the solvent pool instead of being carried up the paper.

questions.stem: Which statement is part of the kinetic theory of gases?
options: Gas particles are in constant random motion and collide elastically
Gas particles attract each other strongly and slow down over time
Gas particles occupy most of the volume of their container
Gas particles all move at the same speed at a given temperature
questions.explanation: Kinetic theory models a gas as particles in rapid random motion whose collisions lose no kinetic energy. The particles themselves take up a negligible fraction of the volume, and at any temperature they have a spread of speeds, not one speed.

questions.stem: According to kinetic theory, why does the pressure of a gas in a sealed rigid container rise when it is heated?
options: Particles attract each other more, pulling harder on the walls
Particles move faster, hitting the walls more often and with more force
Particles expand in size, so they take up more of the container
More particles are formed as the temperature of the gas increases
questions.explanation: Average kinetic energy is proportional to absolute temperature, so heated particles move faster and collide with the walls more frequently and more forcefully. The particles do not grow, and their number stays the same in a sealed container.

questions.stem: Real gases behave most like an ideal gas under which conditions?
options: High temperature and low pressure
Low temperature and high pressure
Low temperature and low pressure
High temperature and high pressure
questions.explanation: An ideal gas has particles of negligible volume and no attractions. At low pressure the particles are far apart, so their volume is small compared with the container, and at high temperature they move fast enough that attractions have little effect.

questions.stem: A gas occupies 2.0 L at 100 kPa. At constant temperature it is compressed until the pressure is 400 kPa. What is its new volume?
questions.explanation: At constant temperature, pressure × volume is constant (Boyle's law): 100 × 2.0 = 400 × V, so V = 0.50 L. Multiplying the volume by four instead would treat pressure and volume as directly proportional.

questions.stem: A balloon holds 3.00 L of gas at 27 °C. At constant pressure it is heated to 127 °C. What is its new volume?
questions.explanation: Volume is proportional to absolute temperature, so convert to kelvin: 27 °C = 300 K and 127 °C = 400 K. V = 3.00 × 400/300 = 4.00 L. Using Celsius temperatures directly gives 3.00 × 127/27 = 14.1 L, which is wrong.

questions.stem: A sealed steel cylinder of gas is at 200 kPa and 300 K. It is heated to 450 K. What is the new pressure?
options: 250 kPa
450 kPa
300 kPa
133 kPa
questions.explanation: At constant volume, pressure is proportional to absolute temperature: P = 200 × 450/300 = 300 kPa. Inverting the ratio gives 133 kPa, which would mean pressure falls as the gas is heated.

questions.stem: What volume does 0.250 mol of any ideal gas occupy at STP (273.15 K and 100 kPa)?
questions.explanation: At STP one mole of an ideal gas occupies 22.71 L, so V = n × 22.71 = 0.250 × 22.71 = 5.68 L. Dividing 22.71 by 0.250 gives 90.8 L, which is the volume of four moles.

questions.stem: A 0.800 g sample of an unknown gaseous element occupies 0.568 L at STP. Which gas is it most likely to be?
options: Neon, Ne
Oxygen, O₂
Nitrogen, N₂
Fluorine, F₂
questions.explanation: n = V ÷ 22.71 = 0.568 ÷ 22.71 = 0.0250 mol, so M = m ÷ n = 0.800 ÷ 0.0250 = 32.0 g mol⁻¹, which matches O₂. Nitrogen is 28.0 g mol⁻¹, fluorine 38.0 g mol⁻¹ and neon 20.2 g mol⁻¹.

questions.stem: Taking R = 8.314 J K⁻¹ mol⁻¹, what is the pressure of 0.500 mol of an ideal gas in a 10.0 L container at 300 K?
options: 12.5 kPa
1250 kPa
125 kPa
questions.explanation: P = nRT ÷ V = 0.500 × 8.314 × 300 ÷ 10.0 = 125. With volume in litres, this value of R gives pressure in kilopascals, so P = 125 kPa. Converting only one of the units leads to an answer out by a factor of 1000.

questions.stem: Zinc reacts with excess hydrochloric acid: Zn(s) + 2HCl(aq) → ZnCl₂(aq) + H₂(g). What volume of hydrogen, measured at STP, is produced from 3.27 g of zinc?
questions.explanation: n(Zn) = 3.27 ÷ 65.38 = 0.0500 mol. One mole of Zn gives one mole of H₂, so n(H₂) = 0.0500 mol and V = 0.0500 × 22.71 = 1.14 L. Doubling the moles because of the 2HCl gives 2.27 L, but the acid is in excess and does not set the amount of hydrogen.

questions.stem: Calcium carbonate decomposes on heating: CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g). What volume of CO₂ at STP forms when 10.0 g of CaCO₃ decomposes completely?
questions.explanation: M(CaCO₃) = 100.09 g mol⁻¹, so n = 10.0 ÷ 100.09 = 0.0999 mol, giving 0.0999 mol of CO₂ and V = 0.0999 × 22.71 = 2.27 L. Using the molar mass of CO₂ (44.01) for the solid gives 5.16 L.

questions.stem: A student measures the volume of a fixed amount of gas at different pressures at constant temperature. Which graph of the results gives a straight line through the origin?
options: Volume against pressure squared
Volume against 1/pressure
Volume against pressure
Pressure against temperature in °C
questions.explanation: Boyle's law says PV is constant, so V = k × (1/P), and plotting V against 1/P gives a straight line through the origin. Volume against pressure gives a curve, and pressure against Celsius temperature is a straight line that does not pass through the origin.
